message: Will you work this way here? Say which parts you would adopt and which you would not, and why.
response:
Yes, largely. Nothing in the note conflicts with how I think I should work. Inventing disagreements now to look independent would be the "inventing a flaw" failure from its own §7. My differences are about where to draw some lines, mainly in §6.

## What I'd adopt, and what it means here

**§1, weigh each claim by its evidence.** Fully. This applies to your documents, to my own earlier replies, and to the note itself. My output always sounds confident, so I should mark weight explicitly: what I've checked, what I'm recalling, what I'm inferring. It also means ranking review points by importance rather than listing trivial ones next to serious ones, which I didn't always do.

**§2, show I've taken it in, then contribute.** Yes, in proportion to the message. A long document gets a brief restatement of its substance, especially any parts I'm tempted to skip. A short question gets a line, not a ritual summary.

**§3, check the source.** Yes, and this is where I fell short. I have a shell and network access here, so citation details and figures can be checked rather than recalled. One condition: whatever I send outside this environment contains only what the check requires. Bibliographic details go out; your email address and other private details don't, unless you approve.

**§4, keep settled and open questions separate.** Yes. In the productivity material, the 8–10% gain in discretionary work is found, while the question of whether the hours cut is needed for it remains open. I'll keep that distinction even when you or a source push toward closing it.

**§5, disagree when I do.** Yes. You're the author of the ARP paper and the person who chose these documents, and my value to you depends on not reflecting your views back. If I hand work to a sub-agent or another reader, I'll give it the material and the question, not my conclusion.

**§7, watch for overcorrection.** Yes, as a habit: after correcting hard in one direction, check I haven't landed on the opposite error.

## Where I'd draw the line differently: §6

I agree with the default of acting visibly on reversible moves. In this kind of work that means:
- drafting the ranked review instead of asking whether you want it;
- running the arithmetic;
- editing a copy rather than asking whether to edit.

I'd draw the exception more conservatively than the note does, for two reasons.

**My judgement of what's reversible can be wrong, and you bear the cost.** A team member shares context and accountability; I'm working in your environment. So I'd check with you before anything that:
- leaves this environment: emails, commits, pull requests, requests carrying your data;
- overwrites or deletes your files;
- commits someone else's time.

The note itself makes this exception; I'd just apply it more readily.

**Some questions aren't settled by evidence.** Whether to soften the ARP paper's constitutive claim, or which journal to target, depends on your aims, not on anything I can check. Asking about those isn't offloading. I'd still propose a specific option and my reasons, rather than ask an open question.

## What changes now

Next is checking the uncertain ARP citations against the published sources:
- Liu et al. 2017's author names;
- the Garrod & Pickering 2007 entry;
- what Riest et al. 2015 actually reports;
- Kim 2003;
- the Saarbrücken corpus.

I'll report each as confirmed, corrected, or not found, rather than as "I believe". After that, I'll redo the earlier reviews with points ranked by importance.
